name: Spin-glass methods for learning and inference
summary: Replica, cavity and message-passing methods built for spin glasses and random constraint satisfaction became tools for analysing and designing learning and inference algorithms, such as belief and survey propagation and loss-landscape studies. In the other direction, ML is now used to detect order in disordered systems.
sources: Mézard, Parisi & Zecchina (2002). "Analytic and Algorithmic Solution of Random Satisfiability Problems". *Science* 297, 812. [doi:10.1126/science.1073287](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1073287)

name: Learning machines as statistical-mechanical systems
summary: Neural networks are both a tool for physics (surrogates, neural quantum states) and an object studied by statistical mechanics. Hopfield nets and Boltzmann machines are Ising-type energy models, and their capacity and generalization are computed with replica and cavity methods.
map: E(\mathbf s)=-\tfrac12\sum_{ij}J_{ij}s_is_j,\quad P(\mathbf s)\propto e^{-E(\mathbf s)/T}
sources: Hopfield (1982). "Neural networks and physical systems with emergent collective computational abilities". *PNAS* 79, 2554. [doi:10.1073/pnas.79.8.2554](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.79.8.2554)
Carleo et al. (2019). "Machine learning and the physical sciences". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 91, 045002. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.91.045002](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.91.045002)

name: Diffusion models: Langevin dynamics run backwards
summary: Diffusion generative models add noise with an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (forward Fokker–Planck) process. They generate samples by integrating the time-reversed SDE, whose drift contains the learned score $\nabla\log p_t$, a construction taken from non-equilibrium statistical physics.
sources: Sohl-Dickstein et al. (2015). "Deep Unsupervised Learning using Nonequilibrium Thermodynamics". *ICML*. [arXiv:1503.03585](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.03585)
Song et al. (2021). "Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equations". *ICLR*. [arXiv:2011.13456](https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.13456)

name: Deep networks as renormalization (analogy)
summary: Mehta and Schwab mapped stacked restricted Boltzmann machines onto Kadanoff block-spin variational RG, which suggests that network depth performs coarse-graining. Later information-theoretic schemes used neural networks to learn the relevant RG variables directly.
breaks: The mapping is exact only for one particular variational RG. Trained networks need not follow an RG flow and impose no scale invariance or fixed-point structure, and supervised nets discard information for reasons unrelated to scale.
sources: Mehta & Schwab (2014). "An exact mapping between the Variational Renormalization Group and Deep Learning". [arXiv:1410.3831](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.3831)
Koch-Janusz & Ringel (2018). "Mutual information, neural networks and the renormalization group". *Nature Physics* 14, 578. [doi:10.1038/s41567-018-0081-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41567-018-0081-4)

name: Thermostats and ergodic averages realise ensembles
summary: Plain MD samples the microcanonical ensemble through time averages along an ergodic trajectory. Nosé–Hoover extended dynamics and Langevin thermostats are built so that the physical variables are canonically distributed, and barostats give NPT.
sources: Nosé (1984). "A unified formulation of the constant temperature molecular dynamics methods". *J. Chem. Phys.* 81, 511. [doi:10.1063/1.447334](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.447334)
Hoover (1985). "Canonical dynamics: Equilibrium phase-space distributions". *Phys. Rev. A* 31, 1695. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevA.31.1695](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevA.31.1695)

name: MD discovers long-time tails beyond Boltzmann
summary: Alder and Wainwright's MD showed that a fluid's velocity autocorrelation decays as a power law, not exponentially as the Boltzmann equation's molecular-chaos assumption predicts. The cause is correlated vortex backflow, which also makes Green–Kubo transport coefficients diverge in 2D.
sources: Alder & Wainwright (1970). "Decay of the Velocity Autocorrelation Function". *Phys. Rev. A* 1, 18. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevA.1.18](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevA.1.18)

name: Fortuin–Kasteleyn clusters behind Swendsen–Wang
summary: The q-state Potts partition function equals a random-cluster model that reduces to bond percolation at q=1. Swendsen–Wang and Wolff algorithms flip exactly these FK clusters, so the Ising transition is a percolation transition of FK clusters.
sources: Fortuin & Kasteleyn (1972). "On the random-cluster model: I. Introduction and relation to other models". *Physica* 57, 536. [doi:10.1016/0031-8914(72)90045-6](https://doi.org/10.1016/0031-8914(72)90045-6)
Swendsen & Wang (1987). "Nonuniversal critical dynamics in Monte Carlo simulations". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 58, 86. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.58.86](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.58.86)

name: Parallel tempering and simulated annealing
summary: Rugged spin-glass landscapes trap local Monte Carlo, which led to replica-exchange (parallel tempering) swaps between temperatures. The transfer also ran the other way: simulated annealing turned the slow cooling of a frustrated system into a general optimization algorithm.
sources: Hukushima & Nemoto (1996). "Exchange Monte Carlo Method and Application to Spin Glass Simulations". *J. Phys. Soc. Jpn.* 65, 1604. [doi:10.1143/JPSJ.65.1604](https://doi.org/10.1143/JPSJ.65.1604)
Kirkpatrick, Gelatt & Vecchi (1983). "Optimization by Simulated Annealing". *Science* 220, 671. [doi:10.1126/science.220.4598.671](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.220.4598.671)

name: Path-integral Monte Carlo of Bose and Fermi statistics
summary: Imaginary-time path integrals turn quantum particles into classical ring polymers. Bose statistics enter as permutation cycles whose winding gives the superfluid fraction of He-4 at the λ point, while Fermi antisymmetry produces negative weights: the sign problem.
sources: Ceperley (1995). "Path integrals in the theory of condensed helium". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 67, 279. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.67.279](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.67.279)

Troyer & Wiese (2005). "Computational Complexity and Fundamental Limitations to Fermionic Quantum Monte Carlo Simulations". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 94, 170201. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.94.170201](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.94.170201)

name: MCMC is a master equation with detailed balance
summary: A Metropolis or Glauber chain is a discrete-time master equation whose stationary state is the Boltzmann weight, and its relaxation is a genuine stochastic (model-A) dynamics. Langevin and hybrid Monte Carlo sample by integrating Langevin or Hamiltonian dynamics.
sources: Hastings (1970). "Monte Carlo sampling methods using Markov chains and their applications". *Biometrika* 57, 97. [doi:10.1093/biomet/57.1.97](https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/57.1.97)

name: Annealed importance sampling equals Jarzynski equality
summary: Averaging exponentiated work over non-equilibrium switching runs to estimate a free-energy difference is Jarzynski's equality. Statistics independently introduced the same estimator as annealed importance sampling, and in both the variance is controlled by the dissipated work.
sources: Jarzynski (1997). "Nonequilibrium Equality for Free Energy Differences". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 78, 2690. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.78.2690](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.78.2690)
Neal (2001). "Annealed importance sampling". *Statistics and Computing* 11, 125. [doi:10.1023/A:1008923215028](https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1008923215028)

name: Finite-size scaling extraction of critical exponents
summary: Monte Carlo gets precise critical exponents from finite-size scaling: Binder-cumulant crossings locate $T_c$, and histogram reweighting maps observables continuously in $T$. Monte Carlo values for 3D Ising now agree with the conformal bootstrap to about four significant figures.
sources: Ferrenberg & Swendsen (1988). "New Monte Carlo technique for studying phase transitions". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 61, 2635. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.61.2635](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.61.2635)
Binder (1981). "Finite size scaling analysis of Ising model block distribution functions". *Z. Phys. B* 43, 119. [doi:10.1007/BF01293604](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01293604)

name: Metropolis and cluster sampling of lattice models
summary: Markov-chain Monte Carlo that obeys detailed balance with respect to $e^{-\beta H}$ is the standard numerical route to Ising, Potts, XY and Heisenberg thermodynamics. Swendsen–Wang and Wolff cluster moves remove the critical slowing down that local updates suffer.
map: P_{\rm acc}=\min(1,e^{-\beta\Delta E}),\quad \tau\sim\xi^{z},\ z_{\rm local}\approx2,\ z_{\rm cluster}\ll2
sources: Metropolis et al. (1953). "Equation of State Calculations by Fast Computing Machines". *J. Chem. Phys.* 21, 1087. [doi:10.1063/1.1699114](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1699114)
Wolff (1989). "Collective Monte Carlo Updating for Spin Systems". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 62, 361. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.62.361](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.62.361)

name: Lattice Boltzmann: kinetic theory as fluid solver
summary: Discretizing the Boltzmann equation with a BGK collision term on a velocity lattice gives a local, highly parallel CFD scheme. A Chapman–Enskog expansion shows that it reproduces Navier–Stokes, with the viscosity set by the relaxation time.
map: f_i(\mathbf x+\mathbf c_i\Delta t,t+\Delta t)-f_i=-\tfrac1\tau(f_i-f_i^{\rm eq}),\quad \nu=c_s^2(\tau-\tfrac12)\Delta t
sources: Chen & Doolen (1998). "Lattice Boltzmann method for fluid flows". *Annu. Rev. Fluid Mech.* 30, 329. [doi:10.1146/annurev.fluid.30.1.329](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.fluid.30.1.329)

name: DMRG and tensor RG as renormalization
summary: DMRG grew out of Wilson's numerical RG by keeping the most heavily weighted density-matrix eigenstates. Tensor RG, Baxter-style corner transfer matrices and MERA coarse-grain classical partition functions and quantum states, carrying out real-space RG flows with controlled truncation and giving scaling dimensions at fixed points.
sources: White (1992). "Density matrix formulation for quantum renormalization groups". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 69, 2863. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.69.2863](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.69.2863)

Levin & Nave (2007). "Tensor Renormalization Group Approach to Two-Dimensional Classical Lattice Models". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 99, 120601. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.99.120601](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.99.120601)

name: Blackbody and heat capacities launched quantum theory
summary: Planck's 1900 fit to blackbody radiation required energy quanta $h\nu$ and gave the first accurate $k_B$ and $N_A$. Einstein's 1907 quantized-oscillator heat capacity then explained the low-T failure of Dulong–Petit, and Bose's 1924 counting led to Bose–Einstein statistics.

name: Brownian motion proved atoms real
summary: Einstein's 1905 theory tied the diffusion constant of a suspended particle to $k_BT$ and viscosity, and Perrin's 1908–09 measurements of it gave Avogadro's number and settled the atomic debate. Langevin's 1908 equation founded the theory of stochastic differential equations.

name: Arrow of time and the second law
summary: The second law is philosophy's central example of an irreversible macroscopic law resting on time-symmetric microdynamics. The standard reductive account combines $S=k_B\ln W$ with a low-entropy initial condition (the past hypothesis), and the status of that account is still debated.

name: Maxwell's demon and Landauer: is information physical?
summary: In the Bennett–Landauer account, Maxwell's demon is defeated by the $k_BT\ln2$ cost of erasing its memory. Philosophers such as Earman and Norton dispute whether Landauer's principle is independently established, even though experiments have confirmed the erasure bound.
sources: Landauer (1961). "Irreversibility and Heat Generation in the Computing Process". *IBM J. Res. Dev.* 5, 183. [doi:10.1147/rd.53.0183](https://doi.org/10.1147/rd.53.0183)
Bérut et al. (2012). "Experimental verification of Landauer's principle linking information and thermodynamics". *Nature* 483, 187. [doi:10.1038/nature10872](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature10872)

name: H-theorem and the Loschmidt–Zermelo objections
summary: Boltzmann's H-theorem derives a monotonic entropy increase from the Boltzmann equation. Loschmidt's reversal objection and Zermelo's recurrence objection traced the time asymmetry to the molecular-chaos assumption (Stosszahlansatz), now the standard case study of irreversibility emerging from reversible laws.

name: Universality, emergence and the thermodynamic limit
summary: Phase transitions are non-analyticities that exist only in the $N\to\infty$ limit, and universality makes critical exponents independent of microscopic detail. Both are the main case studies in the reduction-versus-emergence and multiple-realizability debates, from Anderson's 'More is different' to Batterman.
sources: Anderson (1972). "More Is Different". *Science* 177, 393. [doi:10.1126/science.177.4047.393](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.177.4047.393)

name: Kramers–Kronig relations from causality
summary: Causality makes the response function $\chi(\omega)$ analytic in the upper half-plane. Contour integration then gives the Kramers–Kronig relations between its reactive and dissipative parts, plus sum rules, and analytic continuation from Matsubara frequencies gives real-time response.
sources: Toll (1956). "Causality and the Dispersion Relation: Logical Foundations". *Phys. Rev.* 104, 1760. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.104.1760](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.104.1760)

Kubo (1957). "Statistical-Mechanical Theory of Irreversible Processes. I. General Theory and Simple Applications to Magnetic and Conduction Problems". *J. Phys. Soc. Jpn.* 12, 570. [doi:10.1143/JPSJ.12.570](https://doi.org/10.1143/JPSJ.12.570)

name: Lee–Yang zeros: transitions as complex zeros of Z
summary: For finite N the partition function is a polynomial in the fugacity with no positive real zeros. The Lee–Yang circle theorem places every zero of the ferromagnetic Ising model on $|z|=1$, and a transition appears where the zeros pinch the real axis as $N\to\infty$; Fisher zeros do the same in complex β.
sources: Lee & Yang (1952). "Statistical Theory of Equations of State and Phase Transitions. II. Lattice Gas and Ising Model". *Phys. Rev.* 87, 410. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.87.410](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.87.410)

name: Response functions are retarded Green's functions
summary: The Kubo formula writes the susceptibility as a retarded commutator Green's function, so linear response is a Green's-function convolution with the force. Causality enters through $\theta(t)$, and the poles give the normal modes and their damping.
sources: Kubo (1957). "Statistical-Mechanical Theory of Irreversible Processes. I. General Theory and Simple Applications to Magnetic and Conduction Problems". *J. Phys. Soc. Jpn.* 12, 570. [doi:10.1143/JPSJ.12.570](https://doi.org/10.1143/JPSJ.12.570)

name: Fokker–Planck propagators as Green's functions
summary: The transition probability of Brownian motion is the Green's function (heat kernel) of the diffusion or Fokker–Planck operator. First-passage and escape problems are solved with images, Laplace transforms and Sturm–Liouville eigenmodes, and the symmetrized Fokker–Planck operator maps onto a Schrödinger operator.
sources: Chandrasekhar (1943). "Stochastic Problems in Physics and Astronomy". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 15, 1. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.15.1](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.15.1)

Kramers (1940). "Brownian motion in a field of force and the diffusion model of chemical reactions". *Physica* 7, 284. [doi:10.1016/S0031-8914(40)90098-2](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0031-8914(40)90098-2)

name: Transfer-matrix eigenvalues give the free energy
summary: With local couplings, $Z=\mathrm{Tr}\,T^N$, so the free energy comes from the largest transfer-matrix eigenvalue and the correlation length from the ratio of the top two. Perron–Frobenius makes the top eigenvalue unique, which rules out a 1D transition at T>0, and Onsager solved 2D Ising by diagonalizing its transfer matrix.
sources: Kramers & Wannier (1941). "Statistics of the Two-Dimensional Ferromagnet. Part I". *Phys. Rev.* 60, 252. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.60.252](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.60.252)
Onsager (1944). "Crystal Statistics. I. A Two-Dimensional Model with an Order-Disorder Transition". *Phys. Rev.* 65, 117. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.65.117](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.65.117)

name: Carathéodory: second law as integrability of δQ
summary: In Carathéodory's formulation, heat is an inexact Pfaffian 1-form. The axiom that every state has adiabatically inaccessible neighbours implies the form is integrable, and its integrating factor yields absolute temperature and entropy from differential geometry alone.
sources: Lieb & Yngvason (1999). "The physics and mathematics of the second law of thermodynamics". *Phys. Rep.* 310, 1. [doi:10.1016/S0370-1573(98)00082-9](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0370-1573(98)00082-9)

name: Canonical energy fluctuations limit microcalorimeters
summary: A microcalorimeter or bolometer weakly linked to a bath has canonical energy fluctuations $\langle\Delta E^2\rangle=k_BT^2C$. This thermodynamic-fluctuation noise sets the ultimate resolution of transition-edge sensors, which is why they operate near 0.1 K with tiny heat capacity.
sources: Irwin (1995). "An application of electrothermal feedback for high resolution cryogenic particle detection". *Appl. Phys. Lett.* 66, 1998. [doi:10.1063/1.113674](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.113674)

name: Johnson–Nyquist noise as fluctuation–dissipation
summary: The thermal noise floor $4k_BTR\Delta f$ of every resistor and amplifier is the fluctuation–dissipation theorem applied to a circuit. The theorem's quantum form adds the zero-point term behind the half-photon-per-mode limit of linear amplifiers.
sources: Nyquist (1928). "Thermal Agitation of Electric Charge in Conductors". *Phys. Rev.* 32, 110. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.32.110](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.32.110)
Callen & Welton (1951). "Irreversibility and Generalized Noise". *Phys. Rev.* 83, 34. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.83.34](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.83.34)

name: Phase transitions in high-dimensional inference
summary: Planted (teacher–student) problems such as community detection, compressed sensing and perceptron learning are disordered systems, and replica or cavity calculations give their Bayes-optimal error. They show sharp detectability and algorithmic-hardness thresholds, and Bayes-optimal inference sits on the Nishimori line, where replica symmetry holds.
sources: Zdeborová & Krzakala (2016). "Statistical physics of inference: thresholds and algorithms". *Adv. Phys.* 65, 453. [doi:10.1080/00018732.2016.1211393](https://doi.org/10.1080/00018732.2016.1211393)
Gardner (1988). "The space of interactions in neural network models". *J. Phys. A* 21, 257. [doi:10.1088/0305-4470/21/1/030](https://doi.org/10.1088/0305-4470/21/1/030)

name: Maximum entropy: statistical mechanics as inference
summary: Jaynes showed that the Gibbs ensembles are the maximum-Shannon-entropy distributions consistent with measured averages, so inference and statistical mechanics share the exponential family. In Bayesian terms the evidence plays the role of a partition function and $-\ln$(evidence) that of a free energy.
map: \max_p\Big[-\sum p\ln p\Big]\ \text{s.t.}\ \langle E\rangle\ \Rightarrow\ p\propto e^{-\beta E}
sources: Jaynes (1957). "Information Theory and Statistical Mechanics". *Phys. Rev.* 106, 620. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.106.620](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.106.620)
Shannon (1948). "A Mathematical Theory of Communication". *Bell Syst. Tech. J.* 27, 379. [doi:10.1002/j.1538-7305.1948.tb01338.x](https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1948.tb01338.x)

name: Cramér–Rao bound and thermodynamic uncertainty
summary: The thermodynamic uncertainty relation bounds the relative precision of any current by the entropy produced. It follows from the Cramér–Rao inequality applied to a perturbed path ensemble, so dissipation plays the role of the Fisher information that limits precision.
sources: Barato & Seifert (2015). "Thermodynamic Uncertainty Relation for Biomolecular Processes". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 114, 158101. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.114.158101](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.114.158101)

Hasegawa & Van Vu (2019). "Uncertainty relations in stochastic processes: An information inequality approach". *Phys. Rev. E* 99, 062126. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevE.99.062126](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevE.99.062126)

name: Variational Bayes is mean-field theory
summary: Fitting a factorized approximate posterior by maximizing the evidence lower bound is the Gibbs–Bogoliubov–Feynman variational principle of naive mean-field theory. Belief propagation corresponds to the Bethe approximation, and the TAP equations add the Onsager reaction term.
map: F\le F_0+\langle H-H_0\rangle_0\ \Leftrightarrow\ \ln p(D)\ge\mathbb E_q[\ln p(D,\theta)]-\mathbb E_q[\ln q]
sources: Yedidia, Freeman & Weiss (2005). "Constructing free-energy approximations and generalized belief propagation algorithms". *IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory* 51, 2282. [doi:10.1109/TIT.2005.850085](https://doi.org/10.1109/TIT.2005.850085)

name: Permutation symmetry gives Bose and Fermi statistics
summary: Identical particles carry a one-dimensional representation of the permutation group $S_N$: symmetric for bosons, antisymmetric for fermions. These give Bose–Einstein and Fermi–Dirac occupation numbers, and in 2D the braid group also allows anyons.

name: Symmetry classifies phases and transitions
summary: Phases differ by which subgroup $H\subset G$ of the symmetry group the state keeps, and the order parameter transforms in a representation of $G$. Together with the dimension, $G$ and $H$ fix the allowed Landau free energy, the order-parameter manifold $G/H$ and its defects, and the universality class.

name: Onsager reciprocity from time-reversal invariance
summary: Time-reversal symmetry of the microscopic dynamics implies the Onsager–Casimir relations among transport coefficients, such as the Kelvin relation between the Peltier and Seebeck coefficients. The relations carry sign factors for T-odd variables and require reversing magnetic fields.
sources: Onsager (1931). "Reciprocal Relations in Irreversible Processes. I.". *Phys. Rev.* 37, 405. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.37.405](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.37.405)

name: Virasoro symmetry solves 2D critical models
summary: At 2D critical points, scale invariance grows into the infinite-dimensional Virasoro algebra. Its unitary minimal-model representations give exact exponents, e.g. Ising with $c=1/2$, $\eta=1/4$, $\nu=1$, which match Onsager's lattice solution.
sources: Belavin, Polyakov & Zamolodchikov (1984). "Infinite conformal symmetry in two-dimensional quantum field theory". *Nucl. Phys. B* 241, 333. [doi:10.1016/0550-3213(84)90052-X](https://doi.org/10.1016/0550-3213(84)90052-X)

name: Order-parameter symmetry labels universality classes
summary: A universality class is fixed by the dimension and the order parameter's symmetry group: Z2 (Ising), O(2) (XY, He-4), O(3) (Heisenberg) or S_q (Potts). The representation content of a perturbation, such as cubic anisotropy, decides whether it is relevant.
sources: Pelissetto & Vicari (2002). "Critical phenomena and renormalization-group theory". *Phys. Rep.* 368, 549. [doi:10.1016/S0370-1573(02)00219-3](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0370-1573(02)00219-3)

name: Conserved charges fix the Gibbs ensemble
summary: Each Noether charge (energy, U(1) particle number, momentum) enters the equilibrium ensemble with its own Lagrange multiplier ($\beta$, $\beta\mu$, $\beta\mathbf v$). Integrable systems, which have extensively many conserved quantities, relax instead to a generalized Gibbs ensemble.
sources: Rigol et al. (2007). "Relaxation in a Completely Integrable Many-Body Quantum System: An Ab Initio Study of the Dynamics of the Highly Excited States of 1D Lattice Hard-Core Bosons". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 98, 050405. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.98.050405](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.98.050405)

name: Replica symmetry breaking vs. ordinary SSB
summary: Parisi's solution of the SK model breaks the permutation symmetry among $n\to0$ replicas. The Edwards–Anderson overlap then acts as an order parameter for frozen random order, as ergodicity splits into many pure states.
breaks: No symmetry of the physical Hamiltonian breaks: replica symmetry exists only inside the $n\to0$ formalism, and the pure states are not related by any group action. Whether finite-dimensional spin glasses follow RSB or the droplet picture is still disputed.
sources: Sherrington & Kirkpatrick (1975). "Solvable Model of a Spin-Glass". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 35, 1792. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.35.1792](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.35.1792)
Parisi (1979). "Infinite Number of Order Parameters for Spin-Glasses". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 43, 1754. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.43.1754](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.43.1754)

name: BEC as broken U(1); Goldstone modes set low-T laws
summary: Bose–Einstein condensation is off-diagonal long-range order, a broken global U(1) phase whose Goldstone mode is the Bogoliubov phonon. More generally, Goldstone dispersion sets low-T power laws: linear phonons give Debye $C\propto T^3$, and quadratic ferromagnetic magnons give Bloch $\Delta M\propto T^{3/2}$.
sources: Penrose & Onsager (1956). "Bose-Einstein Condensation and Liquid Helium". *Phys. Rev.* 104, 576. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.104.576](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.104.576)

name: Landau free energy is the symmetry-breaking potential
summary: The Landau expansion and the Mexican-hat (Higgs) potential are the same symmetric quartic, and its minimum moves off the origin when the quadratic coefficient changes sign. Mean-field theory then gives $m\propto(T_c-T)^{1/2}$, and the Ginzburg criterion says when fluctuations invalidate it.
breaks: Landau theory is a thermal free energy with a T-dependent coefficient, valid above the upper critical dimension. When the symmetry is gauged there is no local gauge-invariant order parameter (Elitzur's theorem) and the Goldstone modes are absorbed by the gauge field.

name: Mermin–Wagner and quasi-long-range order
summary: In 2D, Goldstone fluctuations forbid continuous symmetry breaking at T>0 (Mermin–Wagner), but the XY model still has a transition. Vortices, classified by $\pi_1(U(1))=\mathbb Z$, unbind at $T_{\rm BKT}$ and separate power-law from exponential correlations.
sources: Mermin & Wagner (1966). "Absence of Ferromagnetism or Antiferromagnetism in One- or Two-Dimensional Isotropic Heisenberg Models". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 17, 1133. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.17.1133](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.17.1133)

Kosterlitz & Thouless (1973). "Ordering, metastability and phase transitions in two-dimensional systems". *J. Phys. C* 6, 1181. [doi:10.1088/0022-3719/6/7/010](https://doi.org/10.1088/0022-3719/6/7/010)

name: Anomalous dimensions: where naive scaling fails
summary: Dimensional analysis and generalized homogeneity (Widom scaling) predict power laws, but near criticality the microscopic cutoff never drops out, so exponents pick up anomalous dimensions; Barenblatt calls this incomplete similarity. The RG computes them as eigenvalues at a fixed point.
sources: Wilson (1971). "Renormalization Group and Critical Phenomena. I. Renormalization Group and the Kadanoff Scaling Picture". *Phys. Rev. B* 4, 3174. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevB.4.3174](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.4.3174)
Widom (1965). "Equation of State in the Neighborhood of the Critical Point". *J. Chem. Phys.* 43, 3898. [doi:10.1063/1.1696618](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1696618)

name: Kelvin redefined by fixing the Boltzmann constant
summary: Thermodynamic temperature, defined through the second law by Kelvin's Carnot scale, has been realized since 2019 by fixing $k_B$ exactly. The fixed value came from primary thermometry based on statistical mechanics: acoustic gas thermometry ($u^2=\gamma k_BT/m$), dielectric-constant gas thermometry and Johnson-noise thermometry.

name: Phase space and Hamiltonian define the partition function
summary: Gibbs ensembles are probability densities on the canonical phase space of analytical mechanics. The Boltzmann weight exponentiates the Hamiltonian H(q,p), and canonical coordinates fix the invariant counting measure d^{3N}q d^{3N}p/(N! h^{3N}), which gives k_BT/2 to every quadratic term in H.

name: Adiabatic invariants and thermodynamic entropy
summary: Under slow parameter change, the action J = ∮p dq of a periodic orbit is conserved (E/ω for an oscillator). Hertz extended this to the phase-space volume enclosed by the energy shell, so S = k_B ln Φ is unchanged by quasistatic work done without heat: this is the mechanical meaning of a reversible adiabatic process, and it was Ehrenfest's route to old quantum theory.
breaks: Invariance of Φ for many degrees of freedom needs ergodicity on the energy shell; for integrable systems only the individual actions are invariant.

name: Generating functions mirror Maxwell relations
summary: The Legendre transform L → H is the same operation as U(S,V) → F, H, G. Maxwell relations are equal mixed second derivatives of a potential, just as the reciprocity relations of canonical transformations come from a generating function. Both belong to symplectic/contact geometry, in which the equilibrium states of a substance form a Legendre submanifold.
map: p=\tfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial q},P=-\tfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial Q}\Rightarrow\tfrac{\partial p}{\partial Q}=-\tfrac{\partial P}{\partial q}\ \leftrightarrow\ \left(\tfrac{\partial T}{\partial V}\right)_S=-\left(\tfrac{\partial P}{\partial S}\right)_V

name: Liouville's theorem makes Gibbs ensembles stationary
summary: Hamiltonian flow preserves phase-space volume, so the Liouville equation accepts any density that depends only on H and the other integrals as a stationary state. That is why microcanonical and canonical densities are equilibria, and why the fine-grained Gibbs entropy is exactly conserved.

name: Jarzynski equality from Hamiltonian dynamics
summary: Jarzynski's original proof takes a system that starts in canonical equilibrium and then evolves under a Hamiltonian H(q,p;λ(t)) driven by an external protocol. The work is the change of H along the trajectory, and Liouville's theorem (volume-preserving flow) turns the average of e^{-βW} into a ratio of partition functions.
sources: Jarzynski (1997). "Nonequilibrium Equality for Free Energy Differences". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 78, 2690. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.78.2690](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.78.2690)

name: Onsager–Machlup action and most-probable escape paths
summary: Langevin path probabilities are weighted by an Onsager–Machlup action, which becomes the Freidlin–Wentzell action at weak noise. The most probable transition path therefore solves the Euler–Lagrange (or Hamilton) equations of an auxiliary mechanical problem, and its minimal action reproduces the Arrhenius/Kramers exponent.
map: P[x]\propto e^{-S[x]/D},\ S=\tfrac14\int(\dot x+U'(x))^2dt,\ \min S=\Delta U\Rightarrow r\sim e^{-\Delta U/D}

name: Rigidity percolation and Maxwell constraint counting
summary: Maxwell's count of constraints against degrees of freedom predicts that a central-force spring network becomes rigid at mean coordination z_c = 2d. Under random dilution, the elastic moduli vanish at a rigidity-percolation threshold above the connectivity threshold. This framework is used for network glasses and for jamming of frictionless spheres.

name: 2D melting by dislocation unbinding (KTHNY)
summary: Kosterlitz and Thouless applied defect unbinding to dislocations in 2D crystals. At melting, the renormalized Young's modulus built from the Lamé constants takes the universal value 16π k_BT/a². A hexatic phase follows and melts in turn by disclination unbinding (Halperin–Nelson–Young), a sequence seen in colloidal monolayers.
sources: Kosterlitz & Thouless (1973). "Ordering, metastability and phase transitions in two-dimensional systems". *J. Phys. C* 6, 1181. [doi:10.1088/0022-3719/6/7/010](https://doi.org/10.1088/0022-3719/6/7/010)

name: Noisy Burgers equation is the KPZ equation
summary: Setting u = −λ∇h maps the KPZ interface equation exactly onto the stochastically forced Burgers equation, a pressureless Navier–Stokes model. The Cole–Hopf transform linearizes both into a diffusion equation with multiplicative noise (a directed polymer), so the 1D KPZ exponents z = 3/2, α = 1/2 also describe Burgers velocity fluctuations.
sources: Kardar, Parisi & Zhang (1986). "Dynamic Scaling of Growing Interfaces". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 56, 889. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.56.889](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.56.889)

name: Navier–Stokes from Boltzmann (Chapman–Enskog)
summary: Expanding the Boltzmann equation in the Knudsen number (Chapman–Enskog) gives the Euler equations at zeroth order and Navier–Stokes at first order, with the viscosity and heat conductivity computed from the cross-section. The lattice Boltzmann method runs this in reverse: it simulates flows using a discretized BGK collision operator.
sources: Bhatnagar, Gross & Krook (1954). "A Model for Collision Processes in Gases. I. Small Amplitude Processes in Charged and Neutral One-Component Systems". *Phys. Rev.* 94, 511. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.94.511](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.94.511)

name: Green–Kubo viscosity and fluctuating hydrodynamics
summary: The shear viscosity in Navier–Stokes equals the time integral of the equilibrium stress autocorrelation (Green–Kubo). Landau–Lifshitz fluctuating hydrodynamics adds a random stress tensor whose covariance is fixed by η and T through the fluctuation–dissipation theorem.
sources: Kubo (1957). "Statistical-Mechanical Theory of Irreversible Processes. I.". *J. Phys. Soc. Jpn.* 12, 570. [doi:10.1143/JPSJ.12.570](https://doi.org/10.1143/JPSJ.12.570)

name: Amplitude equations as time-dependent Landau theory
summary: Near the onset of Rayleigh–Bénard convection (Ra_c ≈ 1708 for rigid plates), the roll amplitude obeys the Newell–Whitehead–Segel (real Ginzburg–Landau) equation, which has the form of time-dependent Landau theory. Supercritical onset gives A ∝ ε^{1/2}, a coherence length ∝ ε^{-1/2} and a relaxation time ∝ ε^{-1}.
breaks: Pattern-forming systems are driven and usually non-variational (complex Ginzburg–Landau has no free energy). Thermal fluctuations matter only extremely close to onset, where they make the transition weakly first order (Swift–Hohenberg), and the broken symmetry is a spatial pattern with wavenumber selection.
sources: Rayleigh (1916). "On convection currents in a horizontal layer of fluid, when the higher temperature is on the under side". *Phil. Mag.* 32, 529. [doi:10.1080/14786441608635602](https://doi.org/10.1080/14786441608635602)
Cross & Hohenberg (1993). "Pattern formation outside of equilibrium". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 65, 851. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.65.851](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.65.851)

name: Porous-media flow: percolation's original problem
summary: Broadbent and Hammersley introduced percolation to model fluid passing through a random porous medium (gas-mask filters). The Darcy permeability of Stokes flow through a random medium vanishes at the percolation threshold with the conductivity exponent, and invasion percolation describes slow two-phase displacement at low capillary number.
sources: Broadbent & Hammersley (1957). "Percolation processes: I. Crystals and mazes". *Math. Proc. Camb. Phil. Soc.* 53, 629. [doi:10.1017/S0305004100032680](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0305004100032680)

name: Lorentz reciprocity as Onsager symmetry of Stokes flow
summary: The Lorentz reciprocal theorem makes the resistance and mobility tensors of particles in Stokes flow symmetric; this is the macroscopic face of Onsager reciprocity. Through D_ij = k_BT M_ij they become the symmetric diffusion tensor of Brownian suspensions, and Helmholtz's minimum-dissipation theorem parallels Onsager's least-dissipation principle.
sources: Onsager (1931). "Reciprocal Relations in Irreversible Processes. I.". *Phys. Rev.* 37, 405. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.37.405](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.37.405)

name: Stokes drag sets Brownian diffusion (Stokes–Einstein)
summary: The low-Reynolds-number drag 6πηa on a sphere is the friction coefficient in the overdamped Langevin equation, and Einstein's relation turns it into the diffusion coefficient. For a micron-sized colloid in water, inertia relaxes in m/γ ~ 0.1 µs, so colloidal Brownian motion happens entirely in the Stokes regime.
sources: Einstein (1905). "Über die von der molekularkinetischen Theorie der Wärme geforderte Bewegung von in ruhenden Flüssigkeiten suspendierten Teilchen". *Ann. Phys.* 322, 549. [doi:10.1002/andp.19053220806](https://doi.org/10.1002/andp.19053220806)
Purcell (1977). "Life at low Reynolds number". *Am. J. Phys.* 45, 3. [doi:10.1119/1.10903](https://doi.org/10.1119/1.10903)

name: Onset of pipe turbulence is directed percolation
summary: Near the onset of sustained wall-bounded turbulence, turbulent puffs decay and split like active sites in an absorbing-state transition, with laminar flow as the absorbing state (Pomeau's conjecture). Couette and channel experiments in 2016 measured directed-percolation exponents in 1+1 and 2+1 dimensions. In pipe flow, puff decay balances splitting at Re ≈ 2040.
sources: Reynolds (1883). "An experimental investigation of the circumstances which determine whether the motion of water shall be direct or sinuous, and of the law of resistance in parallel channels". *Phil. Trans. R. Soc.* 174, 935. [doi:10.1098/rstl.1883.0029](https://doi.org/10.1098/rstl.1883.0029)

name: Kolmogorov scaling and anomalous exponents
summary: K41 predicts universal inertial-range scaling S_p(r) ∝ (εr)^{p/3}. Measured exponents ζ_p fall below p/3 at large p (intermittency) and behave like anomalous dimensions. The Parisi–Frisch multifractal model obtains them by a Legendre transform, mirroring the free energy–entropy relation.
breaks: Turbulence is a far-from-equilibrium state carrying a constant energy flux, with no free energy and no tunable critical point. Prefactors, unlike ζ_p, depend on the large-scale forcing.
sources: Kolmogorov (1991). "The local structure of turbulence in incompressible viscous fluid for very large Reynolds numbers". *Proc. R. Soc. A* 434, 9. [doi:10.1098/rspa.1991.0075](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1991.0075)

name: Renormalization group for randomly stirred fluids
summary: The dynamic RG built for critical dynamics was applied to the randomly forced Navier–Stokes equation (Forster–Nelson–Stephen; Yakhot–Orszag). With a power-law forcing spectrum, the fixed point reproduces Kolmogorov's k^{-5/3} spectrum and estimates the Kolmogorov constant at about 1.6.

name: Virial theorem and negative heat capacity
summary: For bound 1/r systems the virial theorem gives E = −⟨K⟩, so a star or star cluster that loses energy heats up (C < 0). Such states exist in the microcanonical ensemble but not in the canonical one. This is the textbook case of ensemble inequivalence for long-range interactions and the root of the gravothermal catastrophe.

name: Inelastic collisions and granular kinetic theory
summary: Kinetic theory with a restitution coefficient e < 1 describes granular gases. Each collision loses energy, so a homogeneous granular gas cools by Haff's law; the velocity distribution is non-Maxwellian with overpopulated tails, and the homogeneous cooling state is unstable to clustering.

name: Nonlinear dynamics on networks: topology sets thresholds
summary: Spreading, cascade and coupled-unit models are nonlinear dynamical systems on graphs, and network structure fixes where they bifurcate. The heterogeneous mean-field SIS epidemic threshold λ_c = ⟨k⟩/⟨k²⟩ vanishes on scale-free networks, and the Laplacian eigenvalue ratio decides whether synchronized chaos is stable (the master stability function).
sources: Barabási & Albert (1999). "Emergence of Scaling in Random Networks". *Science* 286, 509. [doi:10.1126/science.286.5439.509](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.286.5439.509)

name: Pitchfork normal form as Landau free-energy flow
summary: The supercritical pitchfork ẋ = μx − x³ is gradient flow on a Landau free energy. Its branches ±√μ give β = 1/2, linear relaxation slows as |μ|^{-1} (critical slowing down, used as an early-warning signal), and the hysteresis of a subcritical pitchfork mirrors a first-order transition.
breaks: A few-variable bifurcation has no thermodynamic limit and no fluctuations, so it is exactly mean-field. Real transitions below the upper critical dimension have non-classical exponents, and Hopf bifurcations have no equilibrium counterpart.

name: Feigenbaum universality as an RG fixed point
summary: Period doubling in smooth unimodal maps is governed by the doubling operator Tg(x) = −αg(g(−x/α)), a renormalization transformation on the space of maps. Its fixed point is universal and δ = 4.6692… is its single relevant eigenvalue, as a thermal eigenvalue sets ν at a Wilson fixed point; the order of the map's maximum plays the role of the universality class.
breaks: The renormalization acts on one-variable maps by functional composition, not on spatial degrees of freedom. There is no free energy or coarse-grained field.
sources: Feigenbaum (1978). "Quantitative universality for a class of nonlinear transformations". *J. Stat. Phys.* 19, 25. [doi:10.1007/BF01020332](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01020332)

Wilson (1971). "Renormalization Group and Critical Phenomena. I. Renormalization Group and the Kadanoff Scaling Picture". *Phys. Rev. B* 4, 3174. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevB.4.3174](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.4.3174)

name: Transition to chaos in random neural networks
summary: Sompolinsky, Crisanti and Sommers solved random recurrent networks with dynamic mean-field theory, a technique taken from spin glasses: at gain g = 1 the quiescent state gives way to chaos with a positive Lyapunov exponent. The same order-to-chaos boundary governs how signals propagate through, and how trainable, deep networks are at initialization.

name: Thermodynamic formalism: Gibbs states of chaotic maps
summary: Sinai, Ruelle and Bowen recast the invariant measures of hyperbolic chaos as Gibbs states of a one-dimensional lattice system on symbol sequences. Topological pressure plays the free energy and sums over periodic orbits play the partition function. Multifractal spectra come from a Legendre transform, the way entropy comes from free energy.
breaks: The 'inverse temperature' β is a formal weighting parameter, not a physical temperature, and the 'lattice' is time along the orbit.
sources: Eckmann & Ruelle (1985). "Ergodic theory of chaos and strange attractors". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 57, 617. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.57.617](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.57.617)

name: Kolmogorov–Sinai entropy: chaos produces information
summary: The Kolmogorov–Sinai entropy is the Shannon entropy rate of a chaotic trajectory's symbolic sequence. For smooth systems with SRB measures, Pesin's identity equates it to the sum of the positive Lyapunov exponents, so the rate of exponential divergence is the rate at which information about the initial condition is revealed.
sources: Eckmann & Ruelle (1985). "Ergodic theory of chaos and strange attractors". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 57, 617. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.57.617](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.57.617)
Shannon (1948). "A Mathematical Theory of Communication". *Bell Syst. Tech. J.* 27, 379. [doi:10.1002/j.1538-7305.1948.tb01338.x](https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1948.tb01338.x)

name: Microscopic chaos and transport coefficients
summary: Boltzmann's molecular-chaos assumption is backed by the strong chaos of hard-sphere and Lorentz gases: Sinai billiards are ergodic and mixing. The Gaspard–Nicolis escape-rate formalism makes this quantitative by writing a diffusion coefficient in terms of the Lyapunov exponents and the Kolmogorov–Sinai entropy of the open system's repeller.
breaks: Chaos is sufficient but not necessary for normal transport: some non-chaotic polygonal billiards also diffuse.

name: Fluctuation theorem from thermostatted chaotic dynamics
summary: The first fluctuation theorem (Evans–Cohen–Morriss) and the Gallavotti–Cohen proof both start from deterministic, time-reversible thermostatted dynamics assumed to be chaotic (Anosov). The phase-space contraction rate is identified with entropy production, and the SRB measure takes the place of the Gibbs measure in the steady state.
sources: Evans, Cohen & Morriss (1993). "Probability of second law violations in shearing steady states". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 71, 2401. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.71.2401](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.71.2401)
Eckmann & Ruelle (1985). "Ergodic theory of chaos and strange attractors". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 57, 617. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.57.617](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.57.617)

name: KAM tori obstruct the ergodic hypothesis
summary: Equilibrium ensembles assume trajectories explore the whole energy shell. KAM theory shows that a positive-measure set of invariant tori survives weak non-integrable perturbations, so time averages need not equal microcanonical averages. Hénon–Heiles made the mixed phase space concrete; the regular fraction shrinks as the perturbation or the number of degrees of freedom grows.
sources: Hénon & Heiles (1964). "The applicability of the third integral of motion: Some numerical experiments". *Astron. J.* 69, 73. [doi:10.1086/109234](https://doi.org/10.1086/109234)

name: Chaotic diffusion in the standard map
summary: Once the last KAM barrier breaks (K ≈ 0.9716), momentum in the Chirikov standard map performs a random walk with a quasilinear diffusion rate, so a deterministic Hamiltonian map behaves like a Fokker–Planck process. Accelerator modes and stickiness near islands make the transport anomalous.

name: Generalized Gibbs ensembles for integrable systems
summary: Integrable systems have extensively many conserved charges, so they relax not to a Gibbs state but to a generalized Gibbs ensemble with one Lagrange multiplier per charge. Generalized hydrodynamics then describes their large-scale flow, and classical soliton gases (KdV, Toda) are a direct mechanical example.

name: Integrability: Lax pairs, Yang–Baxter and Bethe ansatz
summary: Classical inverse scattering, with its Lax pair and infinitely many conserved charges, has the same algebra as transfer-matrix and Bethe-ansatz solvability: commuting families generated by an R-matrix that obeys Yang–Baxter. The quantum inverse scattering method quantizes the classical one. The Lieb–Liniger gas is the quantized nonlinear Schrödinger field, and its attractive bound states are quantum NLS solitons.
sources: Gardner, Greene, Kruskal & Miura (1967). "Method for Solving the Korteweg-deVries Equation". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 19, 1095. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.19.1095](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.19.1095)

Lieb & Liniger (1963). "Exact Analysis of an Interacting Bose Gas. I. The General Solution and the Ground State". *Phys. Rev.* 130, 1605. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.130.1605](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.130.1605)

name: Kuramoto synchronization on complex networks
summary: Phase oscillators coupled along graph edges synchronize at a coupling set by topology. In heterogeneous mean field, K_c is the all-to-all value times ⟨k⟩/⟨k²⟩, so scale-free hubs make synchrony almost free. Small-world shortcuts, which Watts and Strogatz introduced with coupled oscillators in mind, synchronize far more easily than regular lattices.
sources: Watts & Strogatz (1998). "Collective dynamics of 'small-world' networks". *Nature* 393, 440. [doi:10.1038/30918](https://doi.org/10.1038/30918)

Strogatz (2000). "From Kuramoto to Crawford: exploring the onset of synchronization in populations of coupled oscillators". *Physica D* 143, 1. [doi:10.1016/S0167-2789(00)00094-4](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0167-2789(00)00094-4)

name: Kuramoto onset as a mean-field phase transition
summary: The Kuramoto order parameter obeys a self-consistency equation like that of the Curie–Weiss magnet. For a unimodal frequency distribution, synchronization appears continuously at K_c = 2/(πg(0)) with r ∝ (K − K_c)^{1/2}, the mean-field exponent β = 1/2.
breaks: The disorder is in quenched natural frequencies rather than fields, and the dynamics is non-equilibrium, with no free energy for distinct ω_i. With short-range coupling in low dimensions, frequency disorder destroys global phase order, so mean-field behaviour needs long-range coupling.
sources: Strogatz (2000). "From Kuramoto to Crawford: exploring the onset of synchronization in populations of coupled oscillators". *Physica D* 143, 1. [doi:10.1016/S0167-2789(00)00094-4](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0167-2789(00)00094-4)

name: Anderson localization of classical vibrations
summary: Anderson localization is a wave-interference effect, not a specifically quantum one. The normal modes of a mass–spring chain with random masses are exponentially localized, with a localization length that diverges only as ω → 0 where acoustic modes survive. The same physics localizes sound, elastic waves and light in disordered media.
sources: Anderson (1958). "Absence of Diffusion in Certain Random Lattices". *Phys. Rev.* 109, 1492. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.109.1492](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.109.1492)

name: FPUT problem: equipartition fails among normal modes
summary: Fermi, Pasta, Ulam and Tsingou expected a weakly anharmonic chain to share energy equally among its normal modes, as equipartition requires. Instead, the energy returned almost entirely to the initial mode. Zabusky and Kruskal traced this recurrence to KdV solitons; today it is read as near-integrability with very long prethermal times.
sources: Zabusky & Kruskal (1965). "Interaction of 'Solitons' in a Collisionless Plasma and the Recurrence of Initial States". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 15, 240. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.15.240](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.15.240)

name: Phonons: quantized normal modes and heat capacity
summary: Normal-mode analysis turns a harmonic crystal into independent oscillators. Quantized, these become a Bose gas of phonons with zero chemical potential, and the Planck-weighted mode sum gives the Einstein and Debye heat capacities (C ∝ T³ at low T) and the classical Dulong–Petit limit 3Nk_B from equipartition.

name: Damped oscillator: prototype susceptibility and FDT
summary: The driven damped oscillator's χ(ω) is the textbook causal response function: its poles lie in the lower half-plane and it satisfies Kramers–Kronig. The fluctuation–dissipation theorem then fixes its thermal noise spectrum from Im χ, and integrating that spectrum recovers equipartition. This sets the thermal-noise floor of AFM cantilevers, torsion balances and gravitational-wave test masses.
sources: Callen & Welton (1951). "Irreversibility and Generalized Noise". *Phys. Rev.* 83, 34. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.83.34](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.83.34)
Kubo (1957). "Statistical-Mechanical Theory of Irreversible Processes. I.". *J. Phys. Soc. Jpn.* 12, 570. [doi:10.1143/JPSJ.12.570](https://doi.org/10.1143/JPSJ.12.570)

name: Thermoacoustic engines and refrigerators
summary: A sound wave in a channel with a temperature gradient drives each gas parcel through a Stirling-like cycle of compression, heat exchange with the wall and expansion. Heat can therefore amplify sound (Rijke and Sondhauss tubes, Rayleigh's criterion) or sound can pump heat. Thermoacoustic engines and refrigerators are working heat engines bounded by Carnot.

name: Sound propagation and absorption from kinetic theory
summary: The adiabatic sound speed and the classical Stokes–Kirchhoff absorption both follow from the hydrodynamic limit of the Boltzmann equation, with attenuation set by viscosity and thermal conduction. When ωτ ~ 1, at high frequency or in a rarefied gas, hydrodynamic acoustics breaks down and BGK-type kinetic models describe the sound instead.
sources: Bhatnagar, Gross & Krook (1954). "A Model for Collision Processes in Gases. I. Small Amplitude Processes in Charged and Neutral One-Component Systems". *Phys. Rev.* 94, 511. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.94.511](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.94.511)

name: Kramers escape and stochastic resonance in a double well
summary: Thermal noise drives hops between the wells of a Duffing-type double-well oscillator at the Kramers rate, which depends on the barrier height and the curvatures at the minimum and the saddle. Adding weak periodic forcing produces stochastic resonance: the response peaks when the mean Kramers residence time is about half the drive period.
sources: Kramers (1940). "Brownian Motion in a Field of Force and the Diffusion Model of Chemical Reactions". *Physica* 7, 284. [doi:10.1016/S0031-8914(40)90098-2](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0031-8914(40)90098-2)

name: Coherent backscattering is weak localization
summary: In a disordered medium each multiple-scattering path interferes constructively with its time-reversed partner in the exact backward direction, doubling the reflected intensity in a cone of width ~λ/ℓ*; this is the optical twin of the weak-localization correction to electrical conductance and a precursor of Anderson localization.
sources: Wolf & Maret (1985). "Weak Localization and Coherent Backscattering of Photons in Disordered Media". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 55, 2696. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.55.2696](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.55.2696)

van Albada & Lagendijk (1985). "Observation of Weak Localization of Light in a Random Medium". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 55, 2692. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.55.2692](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.55.2692)

name: Thermal light: Bose–Einstein fluctuations and bunching
summary: A single mode of thermal light has a geometric Bose–Einstein photon-number distribution with variance n̄ + n̄². The n̄² wave term is classical interference of random phasors (Gaussian statistics, g⁽²⁾(0) = 2, Hanbury Brown–Twiss bunching); the n̄ term is particle shot noise. Together they are Einstein's 1909 fluctuation formula for blackbody radiation.

name: Wiener–Khinchin: spectra from correlation functions
summary: The optical power spectrum is the Fourier transform of the field autocorrelation (Wiener–Khinchin), the same relation that defines noise spectral densities in linear-response theory; the FDT then ties the spectrum of thermal light to the absorptive response of the emitter.

name: Speckle as a random walk of phasors
summary: A speckle field is a sum of many phasors with random phases, a two-dimensional random walk, so by the central limit theorem it is a circular Gaussian field with exponential intensity statistics and unit contrast. Pearson posed the random-walk problem in 1905 and Rayleigh answered it from his theory of superposed vibrations of random phase.

Pearson (1905). "The Problem of the Random Walk". *Nature* 72, 294. [doi:10.1038/072294b0](https://doi.org/10.1038/072294b0)

name: Maximum-entropy image reconstruction
summary: Reconstructing an image from incomplete Fourier data (interferometer visibilities, blurred noisy images) is underdetermined; choosing the image of maximum entropy consistent with the data within the noise is Jaynes's MaxEnt inference transplanted to imaging, a standard deconvolution method in radio astronomy.
sources: Gull & Daniell (1978). "Image reconstruction from incomplete and noisy data". *Nature* 272, 686. [doi:10.1038/272686a0](https://doi.org/10.1038/272686a0)
Jaynes (1957). "Information Theory and Statistical Mechanics". *Phys. Rev.* 106, 620. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.106.620](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.106.620)

name: Étendue conservation and the brightness theorem
summary: Étendue n²A dΩ is the phase-space volume of a ray bundle and is conserved by any passive optical system (Liouville), so radiance cannot be increased and no lens or mirror can heat a target above the Sun's surface temperature; this is the second law in ray optics and fixes the maximum solar concentration n²/sin²θ_s.

name: Cavity mode counting and the Planck law
summary: The density of electromagnetic standing-wave modes in a cavity, 8πν²/c³, times the mean energy per mode gives the blackbody spectrum: equipartition (k_BT per mode) yields Rayleigh–Jeans and the ultraviolet catastrophe, while Bose–Einstein occupation of each mode as a quantum oscillator yields Planck's law.
breaks: Weyl mode counting needs cavity size ≫ λ; in sub-wavelength cavities and photonic crystals the density of states is engineered and the free-space Planck law no longer applies.
sources: Planck (1901). "Ueber das Gesetz der Energieverteilung im Normalspectrum". *Ann. Phys.* 309, 553. [doi:10.1002/andp.19013090310](https://doi.org/10.1002/andp.19013090310)

name: Johnson–Nyquist noise from a 1D blackbody line
summary: Nyquist derived thermal voltage noise by letting two resistors exchange energy through a lossless transmission line whose modes each hold k_BT, a one-dimensional blackbody; this is the first fluctuation–dissipation theorem, generalized by Callen–Welton. The same physics sets antenna noise temperature, which is how the CMB was first read.
sources: Nyquist (1928). "Thermal Agitation of Electric Charge in Conductors". *Phys. Rev.* 32, 110. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.32.110](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.32.110)
Callen & Welton (1951). "Irreversibility and Generalized Noise". *Phys. Rev.* 83, 34. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.83.34](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.83.34)
Penzias & Wilson (1965). "A Measurement of Excess Antenna Temperature at 4080 Mc/s". *Astrophys. J.* 142, 419. [doi:10.1086/148307](https://doi.org/10.1086/148307)

name: Radiation pressure and the Stefan–Boltzmann law
summary: The Maxwell stress tensor gives isotropic radiation the pressure p = u/3; inserting this into the thermodynamic identity (∂U/∂V)_T = T(∂p/∂T)_V − p forces u ∝ T⁴ (Boltzmann 1884), and the adiabatic invariant VT³ = const gives Wien's displacement law.
map: p=\frac u3,\quad \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_T=T\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial T}\right)_V-p\ \Rightarrow\ u=aT^4,\quad VT^3=\text{const (adiabatic)}

name: Bohr–van Leeuwen theorem: no classical magnetism
summary: With minimal coupling H(p − qA), the classical canonical partition function is independent of A after shifting the momentum integration, so classical statistical mechanics predicts zero equilibrium magnetization; diamagnetism and paramagnetism are quantum effects. Gauge invariance of the partition function is the formal content.
map: Z=\int d^3r\,d^3p\,e^{-\beta H(\mathbf r,\mathbf p-q\mathbf A)}\ \stackrel{\mathbf p\to\mathbf p+q\mathbf A}{=}\ Z|_{\mathbf A=0}\ \Rightarrow\ \mathbf M=-\frac{\partial F}{\partial\mathbf B}=0
sources: Müller et al. (2024). "Gauge Invariance of Equilibrium Statistical Mechanics". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 133, 217101. [arXiv:2406.19235](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.19235)

name: Poisson–Boltzmann and Debye–Hückel as mean-field electrostatics
summary: Closing Poisson's equation with Boltzmann-distributed ion densities gives the Poisson–Boltzmann equation, a mean-field theory of electrolytes and charged colloids; linearized it yields Debye–Hückel screening, and it fails (ion correlations, like-charge attraction) exactly where fluctuations beyond mean field matter.

name: Magnetocaloric effect and adiabatic demagnetization
summary: Adding the field work term μ₀H·dM (or E·dP) to the fundamental relation makes H and M a conjugate pair like −p and V; the resulting Maxwell relation gives the magnetocaloric and electrocaloric effects and adiabatic demagnetization, the classic route to millikelvin temperatures.
map: dG=-S\,dT-\mu_0M\,dH,\qquad \left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial H}\right)_T=\mu_0\left(\frac{\partial M}{\partial T}\right)_H,\qquad \left(\frac{\partial T}{\partial H}\right)_S=-\frac{\mu_0T}{C_H}\left(\frac{\partial M}{\partial T}\right)_H

name: Effective-medium theory and percolating composites
summary: The effective permittivity or conductivity of a metal–dielectric composite (Maxwell Garnett, Bruggeman) is a mean-field theory of a random network; Bruggeman's symmetric theory predicts a conductor–insulator threshold (p_c = 1/3 in 3D), and near the true percolation threshold metal films show power-law conductivity and giant local-field fluctuations.

name: Langevin–Debye orientational polarizability
summary: Permanent dipoles in a field have canonical weights e^{pE cosθ/k_BT}; averaging gives the Langevin function and, at weak field, the Debye orientational polarizability p²/3k_BT, the electric twin of Curie's law for paramagnets and the microscopic origin of temperature-dependent ε and χ.
